title: Bài sưu tầm 222 - Passage 2: Wayfinding Across Open Water: Traditional Pacific Navigation
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 222

Wayfinding Across Open Water: Traditional Pacific Navigation

Paragraph 1. Long before European mariners ventured far out of sight of land with magnetic compasses and brass sextants, Polynesian voyagers were regularly crossing thousands of kilometres of open Pacific Ocean in double-hulled wooden canoes. Stretching from Hawaii to Aotearoa (New Zealand) and Rapa Nui (Easter Island), this vast oceanic triangle was settled systematically over several centuries. Early Western commentators often admired the speed of these outrigger vessels, yet many nineteenth- and mid-twentieth-century writers dismissed the settlements as happy accidents, arguing that crews must have been blown helplessly off course by prevailing winds and ocean currents. Modern computer wind simulations and archaeological evidence have overturned that view, confirming that islanders planned deliberate return journeys across empty water with astonishing accuracy.

Paragraph 2. Without paper charts, metallic instruments, or written logs, non-instrument wayfinders transformed the night sky and the ocean surface into a living map. At the heart of their training stood the star compass—a mental diagram dividing the circular horizon into thirty-two named segments, each corresponding to the point where specific bright stars rose and set. Because stars travel across the sky along curved arcs during the night, a navigator could not stare at a single fixed point; instead, they shifted attention from one rising constellation to the next to keep the bow pointed steadily toward an unseen island. When heavy clouds obscured the stars at dawn or dusk, the path of the sun and the angle of wind ripples against the canoe's lashings served as backup guides.

Paragraph 3. Even on pitch-black, overcast nights when the sky offered no visual cues whatsoever, master navigators continued steering by reading the physical motion of the sea beneath them. Deep ocean swells generated by distant trade winds roll consistently across thousands of miles, bending predictably when they strike an island reef or bounce off underwater slopes. Apprentices spent years sitting cross-legged on the deck of a canoe or floating blindfolded in calm lagoons so they could train their bodies to recognise subtle pitch-and-roll rhythms through the hull, committing dozens of intersecting wave patterns and star bearings strictly to mind. Even the flight paths of land-nesting seabirds—such as terns heading out to fish at sunrise and flying home at sunset—helped sailors detect low coral atolls long before palm trees appeared on the horizon.

Paragraph 4. By the mid-twentieth century, colonial schooling, commercial shipping, and Western navigation gear had pushed non-instrument wayfinding to the edge of disappearance; only a handful of elderly masters remained on remote Micronesian atolls. Determined to test whether traditional methods truly worked on long-haul routes, the Polynesian Voyaging Society built a traditional double-hulled vessel named Hōkūleʻa in the 1970s. Because no living Hawaiian navigator retained the ancient skills, the crew invited Mau Piailug, a master wayfinder from the tiny island of Satawal, to lead the journey. In 1976, relying solely on stars, ocean swells, and bird flight—with every modern watch, radio, and compass locked away—Piailug guided Hōkūleʻa over four thousand kilometres from Hawaii to Tahiti, arriving right on target.

Paragraph 5. That single voyage sparked a cultural renaissance across the Pacific. Although satellite GPS receivers and digital chartplotters are now standard on commercial fishing boats throughout the region, formal academies and community voyaging canoes in Hawaii, Aotearoa, and Micronesia have steadily expanded traditional wayfinding apprenticeships for younger generations. Modern instructors note that learning to read wind, stars, and waves does more than preserve ancestral pride: it forces young people to pay close, patient attention to subtle environmental shifts that electronic screens normally hide.

groups.title: Questions 19–23
groups.instructions:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 222?
In boxes 19–23 on your answer sheet, write: YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

groups.title: Questions 24–26
groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D. Write the correct letter in boxes 24–26 on your answer sheet.

steps: Đoạn 1: astonishing accuracy ↔ remarkable precision (E).
Đoạn 2: keep the bow pointed steadily toward an unseen island ↔ maintain proper directional orientation (B).
Đoạn 3: committing dozens of intersecting wave patterns and star bearings strictly to mind ↔ mental memory (G).
Đoạn 1: blown helplessly off course by prevailing winds and ocean currents ↔ accidental drift (A).
Đoạn 5: sparked a cultural renaissance ↔ triggered a lasting revival (I).

q19.text: Early European observers immediately accepted that Polynesian crews planned intentional return trips across open oceans.

steps: Đoạn 1: Tuy ngưỡng mộ tốc độ thuyền, nhiều tác giả phương Tây thuở đầu lại cho rằng việc định cư là do bị gió bão thổi trôi ngẫu nhiên (dismissed the settlements as happy accidents... blown helplessly off course).
Kết luận: Chọn NO.

q20.text: Using a mental star compass involves switching between moving celestial markers rather than watching a single stationary point.

steps: Đoạn 2: a navigator could not stare at a single fixed point; instead, they shifted attention from one rising constellation to the next.
Kết luận: Chọn YES.

q21.text: Learning to recognise subtle ocean wave patterns takes apprentices significantly longer than memorising star positions.

steps: Đoạn 3: Bài đọc có nhắc đủ cả hai việc (recognise subtle pitch-and-roll rhythms và ghi nhớ star bearings), nhưng hoàn toàn không so sánh việc nào mất thời gian học lâu hơn việc nào.
Kết luận: Chọn NOT GIVEN.

q22.text: The 1976 voyage of the Hōkūleʻa proved that non-instrument techniques could accurately guide sailors over thousands of kilometres.

steps: Đoạn 4: Piailug guided Hōkūleʻa over four thousand kilometres from Hawaii to Tahiti, arriving right on target.
Kết luận: Chọn YES.

q23.text: Widespread access to satellite GPS apps has caused traditional wayfinding schools across the Pacific to close.

steps: Đoạn 5: Dù GPS phổ biến trên tàu cá, các học viện và lớp truyền nghề truyền thống vẫn mở rộng (steadily expanded traditional wayfinding apprenticeships).
Kết luận: Chọn NO.

q24.text: In the third paragraph, how do experienced navigators maintain their course when both stars and the sun are hidden?
options: A. by dropping weighted ropes to measure sea depth
B. by following floating patches of coastal seaweed
C. by sensing how distant swells interact with the canoe
D. by listening to underwater sounds produced by fish

steps: Đoạn 3: Khi trời tối đen nhiều mây, hoa tiêu lái thuyền bằng cách cảm nhận nhịp chao nghiêng của sóng đại dương tác động lên thân thuyền (reading the physical motion of the sea... recognise subtle pitch-and-roll rhythms through the hull).
Kết luận: Chọn C.

q25.text: Why did the builders of the Hōkūleʻa recruit Mau Piailug for the 1976 expedition?
options: A. He was the only sailor who owned an original Polynesian canoe.
B. No local Hawaiian sailor still possessed the traditional knowledge.
C. He had previously mapped the route using modern radio equipment.
D. He was needed to translate ancient written navigation manuals.

steps: Đoạn 4: Because no living Hawaiian navigator retained the ancient skills, the crew invited Mau Piailug...
Kết luận: Chọn B.

q26.text: According to modern instructors in the final paragraph, what is an additional benefit of studying traditional wayfinding?
options: A. It helps commercial crews repair broken satellite receivers at sea.
B. It eliminates the cost of equipping small fishing boats.
C. It allows island nations to claim larger fishing territories.
D. It sharpens awareness of natural details often missed when using screens.

steps: Đoạn 5: forces young people to pay close, patient attention to subtle environmental shifts that electronic screens normally hide.
Kết luận: Chọn D.
